context_blurb:
Put a drop of pond water under a microscope and it comes alive: tiny cells swim, crawl and hunt, and each one is a whole living thing. Your own body is built the other way, from a great many cells that each do one job. Living things also differ in how they get their food.

A unicellular, or one-celled, living thing is a single cell that does every job of life by itself, from feeding and growing to getting rid of wastes. The amoeba crawls by pushing out arms of itself called pseudopods, or false feet. To eat, it surrounds its prey with those arms until the tips meet, closing the meal inside a bubble called a food vacuole, where it is digested. It has no mouth. The paramecium, shaped like a slipper's sole, moves by beating thousands of tiny hairs called cilia, which ripple like rows of oars. To back away from an obstacle, it reverses the beat.

In a multicellular, or many-celled, body the cells specialise: each kind does one job and depends on the others. A muscle cell cut from an arm soon dies alone, though it has a membrane, several nuclei and thousands of mitochondria, the parts that release energy. What it has lost is the blood, pumped by the heart, that brought it food and oxygen. An amoeba finds both by itself.

Nerve cells carry signals, and some are astonishingly long. One nerve cell's fibre can run a metre or more, from the base of the spinal cord, low in the back, down to the foot, so it carries signals along the whole leg. Even the longest muscle cell, which shortens to pull on bones, falls far short of that.

A red blood cell, as it ripens in the bone marrow, throws out its nucleus and most other parts. That leaves more room to carry oxygen, because the emptied cell fills with haemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen from the lungs to the body. With no nucleus it cannot divide, and it lives only three or four months. It has no stiff wall either: it is a soft disc that bends through the narrowest blood vessels.

An autotroph makes its own food; the auto in its name means self. Euglena, a green pond cell that swims with one whip-like tail called a flagellum, is one. Keep a jar of pond water by a sunny window and the Euglena gather on its brightest side, because each one makes its own food from light in tiny green parts called chloroplasts, and swims to where the light is best. Its red eyespot cannot see prey; it only tells the cell which way the light lies. In the dark, Euglena can take in food from the water instead.

Even a plant that eats flies is an autotroph. Each trap of a Venus flytrap is one leaf with two halves that snap shut in about a tenth of a second, yet the plant's green leaves make its food from sunlight, and it can live without ever catching a fly. It grows in wet, boggy ground poor in nitrogen and phosphorus, and its catch supplies the nitrogen that is scarce in its soil.

A heterotroph, whose name means other feeder, cannot make its own food and must take in food made by other living things. Every animal is a heterotroph, and so is every fungus. Linnaeus filed mushrooms and moulds among the plants, but a fungus has no chlorophyll, the green colouring that catches light, and in 1969 Robert Whittaker proposed a kingdom for the fungi alone. Fungi have since proved closer kin to animals than to plants. Many feed on dead remains, but others feed on living plants or animals.

A mould digests its food outside itself and then absorbs it: on old bread, its fine threads pour digestive juices into the slice, break the starch into simpler food and soak that food up. Mould needs damp to grow, but water is not its food, and its tiny spore held far too little to feed it.

Yeast is a one-celled fungus, kin to the many-celled mushrooms and moulds. Wild yeast dusts fruit skins and lives in soil. Unlike a bacterium, a yeast cell has a nucleus, and like every fungus it cannot make its own food. No animal is ever made of just one cell.
